newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Agip pullout cast shadow over Singapore bunkering.
newsitem.headline: Agip pullout cast shadow over Singapore bunkering.

text.p: A decision by Italy's Agip SpA to close its bunkering and lubricant operations in Singapore was the latest sign of Singapore's falling bunkering trade and tightening margins, industry sources said on Friday.
Increased competitiveness in prices and quality from other ports may continue to threaten Singapore's status as the world's busiest refuelling port, they said.
A source close to Agip told Reuters on Thursday that the Italian firm had decided to pull its bunkering and lubricant business out of Singapore by October 31.
"Agip is closing down the Singapore branch by the end of October," the source said.
Agip officials were not available for comment.
"There have been rumours about Agip's pullout recently. The decision could be a combined result of bad profits and its company restructure," said an independent bunker supplier.
Agip plans to assign a local agent to run the company's current lubricating business after closing the office. Its crude operations would continue, industry sources said.

"Agip has been slowing down its activities in Singapore recently, but still this is a surprise that it should actually pull out after being in Singapore for over 15 years," said a trader with a major.
"It must have suffered a lot," the trader said.
Agip recently chartered a 6,000-tonne barge for its bunkering business and has term storage in Singapore for bunkering, traders said.

Amid fierce competition from other regional ports, especially in South Korea and the Middle East, vessels calling at Singapore bought 16.9 million tonnes of bunker fuel in 1996, a three percent drop from a year earlier.
Unwilling to pay high prices, sometimes as high as $15 per tonne above Rotterdam prices, many shipowners only refuel minimim bunker requirements from Singapore, traders said.
South Korea, armed with competitive prices and good bunker quality, has emerged as a main bunkering port in the region. And while sales in Singapore are stagnant, sales in South Korea are growing.

International bunkering demand in 1996 totalled 6.5 million tonnes, up 14 percent from 1995. Other bunkering demand in 1996, including domestic needs, would have added 1.5 million tonnes, industry sources said.
"Singapore bunker suppliers are bleeding," said one trader. "We don't get the profits we used to get before."
"Many shipowners have turned to other ports, so suppliers have to fight for fewer and fewer enquiries," he said.

In Singapore, major oil producers and refiners traditionally sell fuel to independent bunker suppliers at higher prices than those sold directly to shipowners to force the independents out of business.
"But sometimes it's really hard to compete with independents. They just offer unreasonably low prices," said one major supplier.
"The cake is shrinking but more people want to share the cake. That's the situation in the Singapore bunker market," said one trader.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65 8703571)
